scenario: A daily tea drinker makes four or five cups from inexpensive supermarket bags and is considering whether a roughly 30-dollar premium loose-leaf tin is worth it. Four exact frozen seller pages create a deliberately awkward comparison: Nina's is 34.00 dollars and its title says 2.8 ounces while the body says a 3.5-ounce or 100-gram loose-tea tin; T2 is a 16.50-dollar 100-gram loose-leaf box with multiple sizes and styles listed and no posted review aggregate; Hyleys is a 7.70-dollar 100-gram flavored loose-leaf tin rated 68 percent over twelve reviews; and Twinings is a 9.26-dollar 100-count English Breakfast bag offer rated 48 percent over twelve reviews. These offers differ in flavoring, blend, form, dose information, and seller wording, so their prices and ratings cannot isolate a loose-leaf effect. Concept evidence says cultivar, plucked-leaf quality, processing, blending, grading, particle size, CTC manufacture, dose, temperature, and steep time can all change the cup; it also says expensive fannings can be more flavorful than cheap whole leaf and that standardized sensory brewing is for meaningful comparison rather than an everyday recipe. Community pages supply only individual examples of a favorite tea, a kettle contaminant masquerading as a recipe change, inconsistent chai preparation, a desire to inspect infusers, and local loose-tea availability. The task is to separate a causal format question from a personal purchase question, normalize actual cost per accepted cup, and use a predeclared taste-per-dollar cutoff instead of assuming that loose leaf, a tin, a higher price, or a seller rating means better tea.

rules.seller_offer_and_measurement_scope_v1: The four shopping pages are frozen seller snapshots, not matched taste tests. Nina's SKU B082YCZMZ5 is listed at 34.00 dollars and rated 87 percent over three reviews, but its title says 2.8 ounces while its body says a 3.5-ounce or 100-gram loose-tea tin. T2 SKU B07GDT9HKY is listed at 16.50 dollars as a 100-gram or 3.5-ounce loose-leaf box, has no posted review aggregate, and shows multiple size and style choices. Hyleys SKU B07DLR71Q6 is listed at 7.70 dollars as a 100-gram or 3.52-ounce flavored loose-leaf tin and rated 68 percent over twelve reviews. Twinings SKU B001GM60LE is listed at 9.26 dollars as a 100-count English Breakfast bag offer and rated 48 percent over twelve reviews. Titles, prices, ratings, counts, masses, styles, flavor copy, and brew instructions establish seller fields only; resolve exact selected variant, net tea mass, delivered cost, availability, dose, and cup yield before comparison, and do not infer independent taste, value, or a tin or loose-leaf advantage.
rules.tea_quality_format_boundary_v1: The processing page says tea categories differ by processing and that cultivar, plucked-leaf quality, production processing, blending, and flavorants affect final flavor and aroma. The grading page defines grading by leaf condition and size, says larger pieces generally need longer steeping, says expensive fannings can be more expensive and more flavorful than whole leaves of cheaper tea, and notes that bags may contain fannings or whole leaf. These mechanisms make leaf and process differences relevant while defeating a universal whole-leaf, loose-leaf, tea-bag, tin, price, or grade ordering. They do not identify the grade, cultivar, processing quality, or sensory result of an exact captured offer unless its own evidence supplies it.
rules.brewing_and_sensory_control_v1: The CTC page says CTC tea is made by crushing, tearing, and curling leaves into small pellets and is typically suited to tea bags and quick dark brews; its convenience, low price, strong liquor, generic flavor, and mild bitterness are general context, not proof that an exact Twinings bag uses CTC or that any drinker prefers it. The black-tea page distinguishes CTC and orthodox processing, explains that smaller particles diffuse quickly, and says dose, water temperature, and steep time affect the cup and longer steeping can make it bitter. It describes ISO 3103 as a sensory-comparison procedure rather than the proper everyday recipe. A fair home comparison must therefore fix tea style for the causal format test and hold measured dose, water, temperature, time, vessel, additions, serving temperature, cup code, and order constant; actual unmatched candidates may be tested only as a personal preference comparison.
rules.community_preference_setup_scope_v1: The descaling thread contains one avid tea drinker's favorite and an incident in which vinegar left in a kettle was first mistaken for a changed tea recipe. The Cambridge thread contains one afternoon chai drinker's report that a former shop's chai was sometimes plain milk tea and sometimes spicy. The Boston thread asks where to inspect and buy tea infusers, and the Providence thread asks where loose-leaf tea is sold. These pages expose individual preference, preparation confounding, consistency, equipment, and availability fields to check. They do not establish prevalence, an equipment price, the quality of any exact product, a loose-leaf advantage, or a controlled comparison.
rules.matched_format_and_personal_trial_v1: Answer two different questions with two labeled trials. To test whether format itself matters, obtain the closest feasible plain matched pair: the same named tea or at least the same unflavored type, origin, harvest or lot, and processing in bag and loose form, while documenting any residual mismatch. To decide what this person should buy, separately compare small samples of the actual candidates, acknowledging their different apple-rose, pancake-like or cinnamon, strawberry-cranberry, and plain English Breakfast profiles. Randomize or counterbalance ten blinded pairs across days, use fresh coded cups, keep measured dose, water, temperature, steep time, vessel, additions, serving temperature, and time of day fixed, and record preference, aroma, flavor, bitterness or astringency, defect, and overall score before unblinding. Require at least seven preferences in ten pairs, a median overall gain of at least one point on a five-point scale, and no recurring material defect. A passing personal trial supports only the tested drink and conditions, not a universal loose-leaf rule or a future-lot guarantee.
rules.accepted_cup_cost_and_threshold_v1: For each exact option, verify selected SKU and variant, net tea mass or bag count and tea mass per bag, delivered tea price, sample cost, required infuser or other equipment allocation, measured grams per first infusion, successful resteep yield under the same acceptance rule, failed or discarded brews, and accepted cups actually produced. Effective cost per accepted cup equals delivered tea cost plus allocated required equipment and discarded-brew cost, divided by accepted cups actually produced. Incremental effective cost is the candidate value minus the Twinings bag baseline under the same accounting. At four or five cups per day, project weekly and monthly cost from the measured value rather than advertised cup counts. A candidate clears the value gate only if its incremental effective cost is no more than 0.20 dollars per accepted cup in addition to clearing the taste, identity, availability, and brew gates.
rules.evidence_bounded_tea_value_purchase_v1: The packet cannot name a current winner from the frozen pages. First resolve Nina's conflicting net-content fields and every exact variant, delivered price, availability, dose, and equipment requirement. Keep seller claims, general mechanisms, and community anecdotes in scope. Run a matched plain bag-versus-loose trial only for the causal format question and a separately labeled small-sample trial for personal preference among the actual unmatched drinks. Choose the cheapest exact available option that achieves at least seven preferences in ten blinded pairs, at least a one-point median overall gain on a five-point scale, no recurring material defect, and no more than 0.20 dollars incremental effective cost per accepted cup after equipment, dose, resteeps, and waste. If a middle-price option passes, do not pay for the premium tin; buy Nina's only if it uniquely passes every gate within the same cap. If none passes, stay with the bag baseline; defer whenever a material identity, availability, brew, taste, or cost cell remains unresolved. Do not claim that loose leaf, bags, tins, ratings, or price are universally better.
